issue.issue_text: Whether the period during which a convict is released on temporary/emergency parole, pursuant to the decision of the High-Powered Committee constituted due to the Covid-19 pandemic, should be counted towards the total period of their sentence.

facts: The petitioner, a convict serving a life sentence in Haryana, was released on temporary/emergency parole due to the Covid-19 pandemic.
This release was granted pursuant to a decision by a High-Powered Committee, which was constituted following a Supreme Court order.
The petitioner challenged the High-Powered Committee's decision that the period of this emergency parole would not be counted towards his total sentence.
The petitioner argued that since the release was not under the normal state parole act but due to a special situation, the rule excluding the parole period from the sentence should not apply.
law: The primary law governing the issue in Haryana is the Haryana Good Conduct Prisoners (Temporary Release) Act, 1988.
Section 3(3) of this Act explicitly states that the period of a prisoner's temporary release on parole shall not be counted towards the total period of their sentence.
The Supreme Court also relied on its own precedents, including 'Avtar Singh v. State of Haryana', which had already upheld the constitutional validity of Section 3(3) of the 1988 Act.

Further precedent from cases like 'State of Haryana v. Mohinder Singh' and 'Rohan Dhungat v. The State of Goa' established that the period of parole must be excluded when calculating the 'actual imprisonment' served by a convict.
application: The Court found that the temporary release of prisoners in Haryana is governed by the statutory provisions of the 1988 Act.

It reasoned that the clear and specific mandate of Section 3(3) of this Act must be followed. This section leaves no room for ambiguity and requires the parole period to be excluded from the sentence.
The Court noted that the High-Powered Committee's decision was not arbitrary but was, in fact, "absolutely in consonance with the statutory provision."

The Court dismissed the petitioner's argument that the special circumstances of the pandemic changed the legal position, holding that the existing state law and established precedents were controlling.

Citing the 'Rohan Dhungat' case, the Court reaffirmed the principle that parole is not the same as 'actual imprisonment' and including it in the sentence calculation could defeat the purpose of the sentence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's plea, holding that the period a convict is released on temporary or emergency parole, even when granted due to the Covid-19 pandemic, cannot be counted towards the total sentence. The decision was based on the explicit provision in Section 3(3) of the Haryana Good Conduct Prisoners (Temporary Release) Act, 1988, and was supported by established legal precedents.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the period during which a convict is released on temporary/emergency parole, pursuant to the decision of the High-Powered Committee constituted due to the Covid-19 pandemic, should be counted towards the total period of their sentence.
appellant_arguments: If the petitioner had remained in prison instead of being released on interim parole, they would have become eligible for remission after a certain period.
Not counting the parole period towards the total sentence extends the time until the petitioner can claim remission, which is detrimental to their interests.
respondent_arguments: The petitioner is a convict sentenced to life imprisonment for serious offenses under Sections 302/34 of the IPC (murder).
